issues.legal_issue: A statutory requirement to deposit part of an alleged stamp-duty deficit before a valuation dispute is referred for determination is constitutionally valid when it forms part of an economic measure directed at preventing evasion and securing collection of revenue.
material_facts: A sale deed executed pursuant to a civil court decree was presented for registration after stamp duty had been paid in the amount directed by the court.

The registering authority considered the stated consideration substantially below the value indicated by government guidelines and sought a deposit of part of the estimated deficit as a condition of referring the valuation issue to the Collector.
The respondent challenged the deposit condition as arbitrary and violative of constitutional rights.
The amendment was intended to address undervaluation of property and facilitate prompt collection of stamp duty.
issues.conclusion: The deposit condition was constitutionally valid; the appeal was allowed and the High Court judgment striking it down was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Stamp Act treats stamp duty as a tax, and hardship is not a basis for departing from the strict construction of clear taxing language: Commissioner of Income Tax v. Firm Muar, Partington v. Attorney-General, Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar, and Income Tax Officer v. T.S. Devinatha Nadar. A statutory right, including a right of appeal, may be made conditional: Vijay Prakash D. Mehta v. Collector of Customs, Anant Mills Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, Gujarat Agro Industries Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, and Shyam Kishore v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi. The Court also relied on the legislature’s authority over stamp duties and documents under Entry 63 of List II and Entry 44 of List III, and on the presumption of constitutionality and judicial restraint in reviewing economic measures.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_economic_tax: A party challenges the constitutionality of legislation that regulates an economic or tax matter.
predicates.reference_requires_partial_advance_depos: The legislation requires a party to pay part of an estimated liability before an administrative reference can be made.
predicates.measure_addresses_revenue_evasion_or_col: The measure is directed at preventing evasion of public revenue or securing its prompt collection.
predicates.no_clear_constitutional_violation: The challenger has not established a clear violation of a constitutional provision.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an economic tax measure that requires an advance partial payment for a reference, and no clear constitutional violation is established, the deposit condition remains valid.

issues.legal_issue: A court may invalidate legislation only when its conflict with the Constitution is clear, and should uphold a reasonable constitutional interpretation, particularly for economic or tax measures.
material_facts: The High Court had invalidated the deposit condition as arbitrary and beyond the object of the Stamp Act.
The Supreme Court considered the challenged amendment an economic measure intended to prevent evasion and secure prompt revenue collection.
The Court found no clear constitutional violation and emphasized that invalidating legislation is a grave step.
issues.conclusion: The amendment could not be invalidated on the grounds advanced; the Court applied a presumption of constitutionality and upheld the legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the presumption of constitutionality and the requirement of a clear constitutional transgression, as stated in Charanjit Lal Chowdhury v. Union of India, M.H. Quareshi v. State of Bihar, State of Bihar v. Bihar Distillery Ltd., Union of India v. Elphinstone Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., and Kedarnath v. State of Bihar. It endorsed Thayer’s doctrine of judicial restraint, relied on R.K. Garg v. Union of India for greater latitude in reviewing economic legislation, and stated that a court should prefer a constitutional interpretation where one is reasonably available.

predicates.legislation_is_challenged_as_unconstitut: A party asks a court to invalidate legislation on constitutional grounds.
predicates.economic_or_tax_measure: The challenged legislation regulates an economic or tax matter.
predicates.no_clear_constitutional_conflict: The legislation’s conflict with the Constitution has not been established clearly and beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.definition: If legislation is challenged as unconstitutional, regulates an economic or tax matter, and has no clearly established constitutional conflict, it must be upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A registering officer who encounters an instrument that appears not to be duly stamped must impound it and cannot return it merely because the party does not wish to proceed with registration.
material_facts: A sale deed was presented to a registering officer for registration.
The registering authority objected to the amount of stamp duty paid and considered the instrument insufficiently stamped.
The High Court had reasoned that the party could avoid the disputed duty by withdrawing the document.
issues.conclusion: The registering officer was required to impound the instrument and could not return it on the ground that the party might abandon registration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 33(1) of the Indian Stamp Act requires a person authorized to receive evidence, or a person in charge of a public office, to impound an instrument that appears not to be duly stamped. The word “shall” imposes a mandatory duty. A registering officer is in charge of a public office for this purpose.

predicates.document_presented_to_public_officer: A person presents an instrument to an official acting in a public office.
predicates.document_appears_not_duly_stamped: The official considers the instrument insufficiently stamped.
predicates.officer_is_in_charge_of_public_office: The official receiving the instrument is in charge of a public office.

issues.definition: When an instrument presented to a public officer appears insufficiently stamped, the officer must impound it.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitrary or extraneous demand made under a valid statutory scheme may be challenged as an unlawful application of the statute without invalidating the statute itself.
material_facts: The Court considered the possibility that an officer might grossly overvalue property and demand a correspondingly excessive partial payment.
The Court distinguished the validity of the statutory condition from the legality of an individual demand made under it.
The Court stated that a party could seek judicial review of an arbitrary demand.
issues.conclusion: A party may challenge an arbitrary or extraneous individual demand, and a court may set it aside while leaving the statutory scheme valid.
issues.legal_principle: A statute’s constitutionality is distinct from the validity of action taken under it. Arbitrary state action violates Article 14: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India. Accordingly, an arbitrary demand may be reviewed and set aside without declaring the enabling provision unconstitutional.

predicates.challenge_targets_individual_official_ac: The party challenges a particular demand made by an official rather than the validity of the legislation itself.
predicates.demand_is_arbitrary_or_extraneous: The particular demand is arbitrary or rests on considerations unrelated to the statutory purpose.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an individual official demand and that demand is arbitrary or extraneous, a court may set it aside without invalidating the law.
